observations.text: SP, on first exposure to the maneuver, executed the nose-high and nose-low recoveries only with the IP directing the roll towards the nearest direction and the sequence of power and pitch inputs. On the inverted entry the IP applied part of the recovery input, the exit altitude deviating by 400 feet and the exit heading by 25 degrees. Performance is at the code desired for this Training Section but marginal, as the recovery sequence was followed rather than initiated. Unprompted recognition of the attitude and independent initiation of the correct recovery are expected in the following sorties.

SP, applying the briefed recovery sequence, recognized the nose-low attitude and rolled the A/C to level off towards the nearest direction, requiring only the IP's verbal reminder to unload before increasing back pressure. The correction was applied with delay but was completed by SP without the IP taking the controls, exit altitude deviating by 300 feet and exit airspeed by 20 knots, with no A/C limit exceeded. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP identified both the nose-high and the nose-low entries without prompting and rolled the A/C to level off towards the nearest direction, allowing no appearance of stall and no tendency to convert the recovery into a Split "S". Minor errors in the timing of the power reduction were recognized and corrected in a timely manner without the IP's intervention, exit altitude deviating by 200 feet, airspeed by 15 knots and heading by 8 degrees. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP recognized every attitude the IP set, including the inverted entry, and rolled to level off towards the nearest direction promptly and with correct control coordination. All three recoveries were accurate and executed with minimum loss of altitude and without exceeding the A/C limits, exit altitude within 100 feet, airspeed within 8 knots and heading within 4 degrees. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP assessed each entry the IP set against the attitude indicator before any control input and levelled off towards the nearest direction with exceptional precision, at no point approaching stall onset and at no point performing a Split "S". Altitude loss was held to the minimum available for each attitude set, with negligible exit deviations of 30 feet, 3 knots and 2 degrees. The accuracy and speed of recognition exceed the levels expected of a student at this stage of the Training Section. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP, due to a recovery sequence in which back pressure was applied before the bank was reduced, did not roll the A/C to level off towards the nearest direction from the nose-low entry. The pull was continued through the inverted quadrant, so the IP took the controls to stop the developing Split "S" and completed the recovery. Exit altitude deviated by 550 feet from the entry value and the A/C load limit was approached during the pull. The unload, roll, power, recover sequence is to be reviewed before the next sortie.

SP, due to a startle response that displaced the memorised recovery sequence at the nose-high entry, did not initiate the roll towards the nearest direction and made no power or pitch input for about four seconds. Airspeed decayed towards stall onset, so the IP directed each step of the recovery and applied part of the control input, with exit altitude deviating by 450 feet and exit heading by 40 degrees. The recovery was not completed without assistance.

SP performed the unusual attitudes recovery at the code desired for this Training Section, rolling to level off towards the nearest direction on all three entries without allowing the appearance of stall or a Split "S". Recognition of the nose-low entry was delayed and the recovery was completed only after the IP's verbal prompt to reduce power, exit altitude deviating by 300 feet and exit airspeed by 20 knots. Performance is marginal within the standard, since the deviations reached the limits of the code. Unprompted recognition and a faster first control input are expected to improve in the following sorties.

SP recognized each attitude the IP set and rolled to level off towards the nearest direction without prompting, keeping every recovery clear of stall onset and of any Split "S". Minor errors in the timing of the power reduction on the nose-low entry were self-corrected in a timely manner without the IP's intervention, exit altitude deviating by 180 feet, airspeed by 12 knots and heading by 7 degrees. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP, applying an active cross-check of attitude, airspeed and altitude, identified the nose-high, nose-low and inverted entries immediately and rolled towards the nearest direction with correct control coordination. Every recovery was accurate and prompt, executed with minimum loss of altitude and without exceeding the A/C limits, exit altitude within 120 feet, airspeed within 9 knots and heading within 4 degrees. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP treated each entry the IP set as a fresh attitude assessment, rolling to the nearest direction and unloading before recovery on every repetition, with no approach to stall onset and no tendency to convert the nose-low recovery into a Split "S". Altitude loss was contained to the minimum achievable for the attitudes set, and exit parameters were held to negligible deviations of 40 feet, 4 knots and 2 degrees. The precision and speed demonstrated exceed the levels desired for this stage of the Training Section. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP, due to a rudder-led roll input applied at high angle of attack in the nose-high entry, did not roll the A/C to level off towards the nearest direction and allowed the airspeed to decay to stall onset. The IP took the controls to prevent a departure from controlled flight and completed the recovery. Exit altitude deviated by 500 feet from the entry value and the A/C load limit was approached during the subsequent pull. The recovery was not completed without assistance.

SP, due to a false attitude perception that was not resolved against the attitude indicator after the inverted entry, did not roll the A/C to level off towards the nearest direction and rolled instead through the longer direction. The nose-down pitch continued to develop into a Split "S", so the IP directed the roll reversal and applied part of the recovery input. Altitude loss exceeded 600 feet and exit heading deviated by 90 degrees. Reference to the attitude indicator before selecting the roll direction is to be reviewed before the next sortie.

SP, due to a recovery started with back pressure before the bank was reduced, did not execute the nose-low recovery with minimum loss of altitude. Recognition of the error was delayed and the roll towards the nearest direction was completed only after the IP's verbal prompt, with exit altitude deviating by 300 feet and exit airspeed by 20 knots. No appearance of stall occurred, no A/C limit was exceeded and the IP did not take the controls.

SP, due to an interrupted cross-check of the attitude indicator while attention remained on the airspeed during the nose-high entry, did not recognize the increasing bank and delayed the roll towards the nearest direction. The recovery was completed only after the IP's verbal prompt to check attitude, exit heading deviating by 10 degrees and exit altitude by 300 feet. Stall did not appear and no A/C limit was exceeded, but the deviation was recognized and corrected with delay.

SP performed the unusual attitudes recovery within the desired standards, rolling to level off towards the nearest direction on all three entries and keeping every recovery clear of stall onset and of any Split "S". Minor errors in power management were twice recognized and corrected in a timely manner without the IP's intervention, exit altitude deviating by 250 feet and exit airspeed by 18 knots. Performance is marginal for the Training Section, the deviations lying close to the upper limit of the code. Greater consistency in the initial power reduction is expected to improve in the following sorties.

SP recognized each attitude immediately and rolled to level off towards the nearest direction with correct coordination of aileron and rudder, applying the power reduction on the nose-low entry without prompting. All three recoveries were accurate and prompt, executed with minimum loss of altitude and without exceeding the A/C limits, exit altitude within 110 feet, airspeed within 7 knots and heading within 4 degrees. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP assessed every entry the IP set against the primary flight instruments before any control input and rolled to the nearest direction on each repetition, showing no approach to stall onset and no tendency towards a Split "S". The recoveries were executed with the minimum loss of altitude available for the attitudes set and well inside the A/C limits, exit parameters held to negligible deviations of 30 feet, 3 knots and 2 degrees. The precision demonstrated exceeds the levels desired for the Training Section. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP, due to the simultaneous application of full power and back pressure in the nose-low recovery, did not execute the recovery without exceeding the A/C limits and allowed the pull to develop towards a Split "S". The IP took the controls to unload the A/C and complete the recovery towards the nearest direction. Exit altitude deviated by 700 feet from the entry value. The unload, roll, power, recover sequence is to be reviewed before the next sortie.

SP, due to failure to recognise the undesired aircraft state before it developed further, did not initiate a recovery from the inverted entry and held the controls in place while the nose continued to fall. The IP directed the roll towards the nearest direction and applied part of the control input to complete the recovery, exit altitude deviating by 800 feet and exit airspeed by 60 knots. The recovery was not completed without assistance.

SP, due to a roll executed towards the longer direction from the nose-high entry, did not roll the A/C to level off towards the nearest direction. The error was recognized late and reversed only after the IP's verbal prompt, with exit altitude deviating by 300 feet and exit heading by 10 degrees. Stall did not appear and the IP did not take the controls, but the correction was applied with delay.

SP, due to an aircraft state that had diverged from the SP's mental model without being reassessed against the attitude indicator, did not identify the nose-low entry as nose-low and initially increased power instead of reducing it. The recovery was completed only after the IP's verbal prompt to check attitude and power, exit airspeed deviating by 20 knots and exit altitude by 300 feet. Recognition and correction were achieved by SP, but with delay and without independent initiation.

SP, due to a late power reduction in the nose-low recovery, did not execute the recovery with the minimum loss of altitude available for the attitude set. The error was recognized and corrected in a timely manner without the IP's intervention, exit airspeed deviating by 16 knots and exit altitude by 220 feet. The roll towards the nearest direction was correctly selected on all three entries and no A/C limit was exceeded.

SP, due to an interrupted cross-check between the attitude indicator and the altimeter during the nose-high recovery, did not arrest the resulting descent at the planned exit altitude. The deviation was recognized and corrected in a timely manner without the IP's intervention, exit altitude deviating by 240 feet and exit heading by 8 degrees. No appearance of stall occurred and the roll towards the nearest direction was correctly selected on every entry.

SP executed the nose-high, nose-low and inverted recoveries accurately and promptly, rolling to level off towards the nearest direction and holding exit altitude within 140 feet, airspeed within 9 knots and heading within 5 degrees. Performance meets the desired standards, but the values lie at the upper end of the code and the first control input on the inverted entry was slower than on the preceding repetitions. Marginal performance for the Training Section; faster and more consistent initiation of the recovery is expected to improve in the following sorties.

SP identified every attitude the IP set on the first instrument reference and rolled to the nearest direction with exceptional control precision, at no point approaching stall onset and at no point converting the nose-low recovery into a Split "S". Altitude loss was held to the minimum available for each entry and well inside the A/C limits, exit parameters remaining at negligible deviations of 30 feet, 2 knots and 1 degree. The accuracy and speed shown exceed the levels desired for a student in this Training Section. Above end of block MIF achieved.
